title: Alvarez II.6: power to the contrary stands with predetermination in the divided sense; the omitter sins by his own fault
source_text: XXV. Ejusdem vero libri cap. 6. Responsione ad secundum argumentum, ex eo quod Deus aliquem praedeterminavit ad hoc, vel illud volendum, negat sequi quod absolute loquendo, non sit in potestate ejus aliud velle, quamvis ex suppositione divinae illius praedeterminationis, impossibile sit, in sensu composito, quod velit aliud objectum. Uno verbo distinguit inter velle & operari, & posse velle atque operari; & concedit absque influxu illo praedeterminante voluntatem nunquam operari, cum eo vero voluntatem nunquam non operari: sed pertendit, cum illo voluntatem habere potestatem non operandi, & contra absque illo voluntatem habere potestatem operandi, scilicet in sensu diviso. Nimirum ex ejus mente, cum influxu isto praedeterminante stat potentia voluntatis ad non agendum, aut aliter agendum; non stat vero actus oppositus, aut cessatio ab actu. Et vice versa, absque illo influxu manet in voluntate potentia agendi, licet absque illo nunquam in actum educatur. Inde autem colligit fieri ut omittens actum qui est in praecepto libere illum omittat, & peccet; quia per auxilium sufficiens poterat implere illud praeceptum; ex Dei autem misericordia poterat habere motionem illam ad agendum necessariam, sua vero culpa impedivit ne illi donaretur a Deo.
pass_a_gloss: But in chap. 6 of the same book, in the Answer to the second argument, he denies that from this that God has predetermined someone to willing this, or that, it follows that absolutely speaking, it is not in his power to will something else, although from the supposition of that divine predetermination, it is impossible, in the composed sense, that he will another object. In a word he distinguishes between to will and to operate, and to be able to will and operate; and grants that without that predetermining influence the will never operates, but with it the will never fails to operate: but he contends, that with it the will has the power of not operating, and on the contrary without it the will has the power of operating, namely in the divided sense. Namely according to his mind, with that predetermining influence stands the potency of the will to not acting, or acting otherwise; but the opposite act does not stand, or cessation from the act. And vice versa, without that influence there remains in the will the potency of acting, although without it it is never brought out into act. But thence he gathers that it comes about that one omitting an act which is in precept omits it freely, and sins; because through sufficient help he could fulfil that precept; but from the mercy of God he could have that motion necessary for acting, but by his own fault he hindered that it should be given him by God.
pass_b_english: In chapter 6 of the same book, answering the second argument, he denies that because God has predetermined someone to will this or that, it is not, absolutely speaking, in his power to will something else, although on the supposition of that divine predetermination it is impossible, in the composite sense, for him to will another object.

In short, he distinguishes between willing and acting on the one hand and being able to will and act on the other. He grants that without that predetermining influence the will never acts, and that with it the will always acts. But he insists that with it the will has the power not to act, and without it the will has the power to act, in the divided sense. On his view the will's power not to act or to act otherwise coexists with the predetermining influence, but the opposite act, or ceasing from the act, does not. Conversely, without that influence the power to act remains in the will, though without it that power is never brought into act.

From this he concludes that someone who omits an act that is commanded omits it freely and sins. Through sufficient help he could have kept the command; by God's mercy he could have had the motion needed to act; and by his own fault he prevented God from giving it to him.

lemmas.latin: velle & operari, & posse velle atque operari
lemmas.gloss: to will and to operate, and to be able to will and operate

choices.why: Kept as the Thomist technical term; Le Blanc explains 'physical' as opposed to 'moral', not to 'supernatural'.
